purpose: This medication is most commonly used to prevent pregnancy. It can also help regulate your menstrual cycle, reduce painful or heavy periods, and is sometimes prescribed to treat acne in women. Your doctor may have prescribed it for one or more of these reasons.
how_it_works: This pill contains two hormones — estrogen and progestin — that work together to prevent pregnancy in a few ways. First, they stop your ovaries from releasing an egg each month. They also thicken the mucus in your cervix so sperm have a harder time getting through, and they thin the lining of your uterus so a fertilized egg is less likely to attach.
common_side_effects: Some women notice nausea, breast tenderness, headaches, or spotting between periods, especially in the first few months. You might also notice mood changes, decreased sex drive, or slight bloating. Most of these side effects tend to improve after the first 2 to 3 months as your body adjusts.
warnings: This medication carries a small but serious risk of blood clots, stroke, or heart attack, especially if you smoke and are over 35 years old — so it is very important not to smoke while taking this pill. Tell your doctor if you have a history of high blood pressure, migraines with aura, liver problems, or blood clots. This pill does NOT protect you from sexually transmitted infections. If you miss pills, your protection against pregnancy goes down.
typical_dosing: You take one pill by mouth every day at the same time each day. Most packs are 28 days — 21 active hormone pills followed by 7 reminder pills (or placebo pills). You will usually get your period during those last 7 days. Try to take it at the same time every day to keep it working its best and to reduce nausea.
